Article Title: In 2021, a landslide cut Denali National Park’s only road in two; five years later a $230 million, 475-foot bridge has been built directly above the still-moving slope
Article Text:
Pretty Rocks bridge (Image Credit: National Park Service)

The landslide that changed Denali

Building above moving ground

A bridge assembled in Alaska

More than just a bridge

Access returns gradually

A long-term solution

In August 2021, a massive landslide in Denali National Park and Preserve tore apart a section of the park's only road, cutting off vehicle access to destinations deep inside the Alaska wilderness. Five years later, a new bridge now spans the unstable ground where the road once crossed the slope. As reported by Alaska Public Media, the completion of the Pretty Rocks Bridge marks a major step toward restoring full use of the Denali Park Road. According to the National Park Service (NPS), the roughly $230 million project includes a 475-foot steel truss bridge built across the active landslide near Mile 45. The bridge reconnects the eastern and western portions of the road and is designed as a long-term solution rather than another attempt to keep rebuilding a roadway across moving ground. Full bus service to the western end is expected to return during the 2027 visitor season.The Pretty Rocks landslide forced the NPS to close the Denali Park Road in August 2021. The failure occurred in the Polychrome area, near Mile 45, disrupting access to some of the park's most important destinations west of the slide. Among the areas affected were the Eielson Visitor Center, Wonder Lake and Kantishna, along with residential, maintenance and privately operated tourism facilities.For several years, park buses could travel only as far as East Fork, around Mile 43. The problem was not simply a section of damaged pavement that could be repaired and reopened. The ground beneath the road remained unstable and continued moving, making repeated reconstruction of the roadway a difficult long-term solution.Instead of building another road directly across the landslide, engineers developed a plan to span the unstable area with a bridge. The result is a steel truss structure approximately 475 feet long, 50 feet tall and 24 feet wide. It was designed to carry the park road across the active slide while avoiding direct reliance on the unstable ground underneath. The project presented unusual engineering challenges. Crews had to work in steep terrain with complex geology, permafrost and a short Alaska construction season. The remote location also made transporting equipment and completing construction more complicated than a conventional bridge project.One of the most striking parts of the project was how the bridge was put into position. Rather than building the entire structure across the landslide, crews assembled the bridge on the east side of the unstable area. In 2025, the completed structure was gradually launched across the slide toward the opposite side. The bridge reached the receiving tower in August 2025 and was subsequently lowered into its final position. NPS described the successful launch as one of the major accomplishments of that year's construction season. The structure also incorporates 23 thermosiphons, underground devices designed to help keep the permafrost beneath the eastern end of the bridge frozen. Maintaining stable ground around the bridge is an important part of ensuring its long-term performance.The Pretty Rocks project involved more than constructing the main span. Crews also worked on road approaches, retaining structures and slope stabilisation. In 2026, workers completed additional construction around the bridge and carried out rock scaling on slopes in the Polychrome area to reduce the risk of unstable rock falling onto the road. A separate section near the Bear Cave landslide was also rerouted away from unstable ground. Construction was declared complete in late August 2026, with final restoration and removal of construction equipment continuing afterward.The completed bridge does not mean every type of traffic immediately returned to the entire road. According to the National Park Service, hikers and cyclists can now travel west of East Fork and cross the new bridge, while park buses remain restricted to East Fork for the rest of the 2026 season. Full bus service along the Denali Park Road will resume in 2027. That reopening will restore access to the western reaches of Denali that have been difficult or impossible for many visitors to reach since the 2021 landslide.The Pretty Rocks Bridge represents a major change in how Denali's unstable terrain is being managed. Instead of repeatedly trying to hold a road in place across an active landslide, engineers built a structure that passes over the moving ground. The approximately $230 million project was funded through a combination of federal transportation, disaster supplemental and infrastructure funding. Five years after the Pretty Rocks landslide disrupted Denali's only road, the new bridge provides a connection across the unstable slope. Its completion marks the end of one of the park's most challenging infrastructure projects and sets the stage for visitors to once again travel farther into Denali beginning in 2027.
Article Summary: A massive landslide in Denali National Park and Preserve closed the park's only road in August 2021. Five years later, a new bridge now spans the unstable ground where the road once crossed the slope. Full bus service to the western end of the park is expected to return during the 2027 visitor season.

Article Title: A 674-acre Colorado ranch was listed for $5.9 million as a development site; conservationists bought it instead, permanently protecting land that links to more than 100,000 acres of public space
Article Text:
The ranch is near the proposed Ring the Peak trail system.

Why Pinestone Ranch matters

Part of a bigger plan

A growing open space

A 674-acre ranch on the northern flank of Colorado’s Pikes Peak, once listed as a development site for $5.9 million, has now been bought by Palmer Land Conservancy and will be protected for conservation.The Conservancy closed on the purchase of Pinestone Ranch on August 11, according to Pikes Peak Outdoor Recreation Alliance. The sale price was not disclosed. The property, located just south of Woodland Park along Old Crystola Canyon Road, contains conifer and aspen forest.The conservation group said it bought the ranch as part of efforts to protect open land around Pikes Peak. The property is next to Pike National Forest and connects Woodland Park with more than 100,000 acres of public land. It also borders the 6,000-acre Pikes Peak Conservation Corridor.For now, the land will remain closed to the public. Palmer will temporarily hold the property while its partners work out long-term ownership and stewardship plans. The group said public access could still be years away, but the conservation protection is permanent.Rebecca Jewett, president and CEO of Palmer Land Conservancy, said opportunities to protect open space on this scale are becoming limited.“There are very few chances left to create public open space at this scale on the Front Range. When an opportunity like Pinestone Ranch comes along, you don’t just protect it. You protect everything it can become,” Jewett said.The ranch is also important because of its location near the proposed Ring the Peak trail system. Ring the Peak is a roughly 63-mile loop around Pikes Peak and is about 80% complete.Pinestone Ranch sits near one of the remaining gaps on the northeastern side of the route, close to Ute Pass. Conservationists see the property as a possible new access point between Woodland Park and the surrounding forest.The site could eventually provide trails, wildlife habitat and a connection between the town and nearby public lands. Palmer said the property could become an important community connector as plans for the wider area develop.The Pinestone Ranch purchase comes as several agencies and organisations are working on a broader plan for recreation and conservation around Pikes Peak.Colorado Parks and Wildlife is expanding its role on the mountain through a partnership involving the US Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, Colorado Springs Utilities and local governments. One of the priorities is to complete and manage the Ring the Peak corridor.The partnership is intended to bring different agencies together instead of having recreation and conservation managed through separate jurisdictions.A $2.5 million Great Outdoors Colorado-Colorado Parks and Wildlife grant is already supporting trail realignments, environmental reviews and habitat work. Pinestone Ranch adds a large protected property on the Woodland Park side to that wider effort.According to Gov. Jared Polis, the partnership would improve and expand recreation opportunities including camping, fishing and hiking while benefiting the landscape and local economy.The ranch purchase also follows several recent efforts to protect or acquire open space around Woodland Park. The town acquired Avenger Open Space in 2024 and purchased the Shining Mountain Golf Course in 2025. Pinestone Ranch is more than five times the size of Avenger Open Space.Woodland Park's parks master plan has identified a connection between the town and the Ring the Peak route. The Pinestone property could provide that connection on a much larger scale.Jewett said the organisation bought the property with the intention of developing a long-term public access vision, particularly because of its location near the Highway 24 corridor.According to Axios, the conservation group is also involved in protecting 1,018-acre Wild Horse Ranch, on the eastern side of Colorado Springs, through a conservation easement.That property is near Corral Bluffs and Jimmy Camp Creek Open Spaces. Together, the protected areas create a wildlife corridor covering more than 2,000 acres.Pinestone Ranch itself is home to habitat for 63 species of conservation interest. Its protection means the large tract will remain intact while plans for future public access and recreation are developed.
Article Summary: Pinestone Ranch is near the proposed Ring the Peak trail system. Conservationists see the property as a possible new access point between Woodland Park and the surrounding forest. The site could eventually provide trails, wildlife habitat and a connection between the town and nearby public lands.

Article Title: In 2013, a UK beach began planting discarded Christmas trees to trap blowing sand; by 2026, the project had created 90 metres of new dunes that help defend homes from flooding
Article Text:
More than 2,000 Christmas trees were planted at St Annes beach in February 2026. (Photo: .visitstannes.info)

Christmas trees build dunes

Why dunes matter

A habitat for plants and wildlife

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of the Fylde Sand Dunes Project do you find most appealing? Discarded Christmas trees are being used to help protect homes and businesses along the Fylde Coast in Lancashire, UK. Since the project began in 2013, old Christmas trees have been placed on St Annes beach to trap wind-blown sand and help build wider sand dunes.According to Fydle Council, the annual work is part of the Fylde Sand Dunes Project, which aims to restore and conserve the coastal dunes. Fylde Council, Lancashire Wildlife Trust and Blackpool Council work together on the project, which is funded by the Environment Agency.The idea is simple. Trees are placed in front of the existing dunes, where their branches slow down the wind and trap sand. As more sand collects around the trees, the mound grows and can eventually become part of a new dune.The project has already produced a visible change. Last year, more than 2,000 Christmas trees were collected from residents and used in the planting work. According to the council, this helped create a 90-metre increase in the width of the Fylde Sand Dune system.Sand dunes naturally develop when wind-blown sand is trapped by an obstruction on the beach. At first, the collected sand can be unstable and may collapse.Plants can then begin growing in small pockets of sand and help hold the material in place.At St Annes, discarded Christmas trees act as the first obstruction. Their branches catch sand carried inland by the wind. Over time, more sand becomes trapped around the trees, allowing the dune to grow.The process then continues naturally. Pioneer grasses such as sand couch and lyme grass can grow in the dunes. Marram grass can later become more dominant as sand builds around it. Its growth helps stabilise the new dune, allowing more plants to establish.As the plants grow and spread, they help hold more sand in place. Eventually, organic matter from plants that die and decay builds up. The dune becomes more stable and develops into a habitat with different plants and animals.Dunes act as a natural, or ‘soft’, sea defence. During storms, they absorb some of the energy from the sea. Wider dunes are more effective at providing this protection. The dunes help reduce the risk of erosion caused by storm surges, which happen when strong winds combine with high tides.However, the dunes along the Fylde Coast are much smaller than they once were. According to the Fylde Council, more than 80% of the dunes have been lost over the past 150 years because of coastal development.The remaining dunes are now squeezed between the sea and nearby towns. This makes protecting and extending them important for both coastal communities and wildlife.Amy Pennington, Lancashire Wildlife Trust’s Fylde Sand Dunes Project Senior Engagement Officer, said the dunes provide habitat for a wide range of plants and animals and also act as a soft sea defence.“The sand dunes along the Fylde Coast are home to a diverse and specialised ecosystem, hosting a variety of unique plants and animals,” she said.The dunes have been designated as a Biological Heritage Site and are also a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). They support specialised plants and animals that are adapted to the dry and shifting conditions of a sand dune environment.Species found in the dunes include dune helleborine orchids, Isle of Man cabbage, dune pansies, sea holly and round-leaved wintergreen. Wildlife includes the grayling butterfly, mining bees, common lizards, skylarks, linnets and reed buntings.The environment changes as the dunes develop. Areas closer to the beach can have alkaline conditions because the sand contains pieces of sea shells. Further inland, the ground can become more acidic as the dune matures, allowing different plants to grow.As part of the project, volunteers also remove invasive plants, plant dune grasses and install paling fences to trap wind-blown sand. In addition, wetland ‘slacks’ are being created behind some dunes to support more plants and wildlife.According to Councillor Tommy Threlfall, Fylde Council’s Lead Member for Environment, the project had continued for more than a decade.“Every Christmas tree donated by our residents becomes part of something truly special,” he said. “We’re not just recycling trees, we’re building natural defences that will protect our coastal communities for generations to come,” he added.The project continues to rely on volunteers and local support. In February 2026, volunteers from across Lancashire were due to gather at St Annes beach to plant more than 2,000 donated Christmas trees.
Article Summary: Discarded Christmas trees are being used to help protect homes and businesses along the Fylde Coast in Lancashire, UK. Trees are placed in front of existing dunes, where their branches slow down the wind and trap sand. As more sand collects around the trees, the mound grows and can eventually become part of a new dune.

Article Title: Four private Michigan islands spanning 520 acres hit the market for $2.3 million; the deal includes a home, two boats and land protected by a conservation easement
Article Text:
Turnkey residence with panoramic water views

Environmental protection and native wildlife corridors

Remote border real estate market dynamics

A private group of four islands covering 520 acres along the US-Canada border has been listed for $2.3 million. The sale includes a renovated home, machinery, two boats and a mainland dock slip. Located in Potagannissing Bay and the St Marys River near Drummond Island, the property includes Burnt Island, Wilson Island, Claw Island and Harris Island, according to the New York Post and listing brokers Coldwell Banker Schmidt Realtors and @properties. Burnt Island makes up most of the property and contains the main home and other facilities. Wilson, Claw and Harris Islands form a smaller group nearby. The large estate combines private wilderness with permanent conservation protections and offers about 2,000 feet of waterfront along northern Michigan’s international water boundary.The main home sits on the southern tip of Burnt Island and offers 270-degree views of the surrounding waterways and shipping lanes. Originally built as an island retreat, the 2,131-square-foot house was fully renovated inside and outside between 2017 and 2018. The home has three bedrooms and two full bathrooms. It is being sold turnkey, with furnishings and working equipment included in the sale. "If you have ever dreamed of owning your own island, here's your chance to own four!" the listing from Gaslight Group Properties and Coldwell Banker says."Set along the picturesque northern border in the St Mary's River & Potagannissing Bay, this group of islands is truly special." The sale also includes a utility truck, a Kubota tractor with a brush hog attachment, a riding lawn mower, a separate sauna building and two motorboats to help with maintenance and travel between the islands. The property’s two main docks and protective breakwalls were rebuilt between 2022 and 2023. The sale also comes with a dedicated boat slip at DeTour Village on the Michigan mainland, providing regular access to the islands.One of the main features of the 520-acre property is the balance between private use and long-term environmental protection. About 420 acres across the four islands are covered by a permanent conservation easement held by the Little Traverse Conservancy, a regional land trust in northern Michigan. The easement prevents future commercial subdivision and major construction, helping protect native forests and wildlife habitats. The owner still has about 100 acres of unrestricted land around the home, outbuildings and shorelines for private recreation and personal use. "Most of the 520 acres is protected by a conservation easement with Little Traverse Conservancy but about 100 of the acres and the shorelines are yours to explore," according to the official Northern Michigan MLS listing. The islands feature private walking trails, wild fruit orchards with apple and crabapple trees, milkweed meadows and quiet coves. Wildlife commonly seen on the islands and nearby waters includes bald eagles, sandhill cranes, red foxes, otters, beavers, coyotes and white-tailed deer. The waters around Potagannissing Bay are also an established fishing area, supporting native populations of walleye, smallmouth bass, yellow perch and cisco.The property is a rare offering in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where large groups of privately owned islands rarely come up for sale. Located about 2,000 feet from the official maritime border between the United States and Canada, the islands offer privacy while remaining close to major Great Lakes shipping routes. People staying on Burnt Island can often watch commercial Great Lakes freighters travelling through the nearby St Marys River channel, which connects Lake Superior with Lake Huron. Real estate agents who specialise in northern Michigan waterfront properties say turnkey island estates with mainland facilities, such as dedicated marina slips, can command higher prices because of the challenges of maintaining remote properties. Listing agents Sam DeCamp and Anna DeCamp of Gaslight Group Properties are continuing to show the property to potential buyers looking for private conservation retreats.
Article Summary: The property is a rare offering in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where large groups of privately owned islands rarely come up for sale. Located about 2,000 feet from the official maritime border between the United States and Canada, the islands offer privacy while remaining close to major Great Lakes shipping routes. Wildlife commonly seen on the islands and nearby waters includes bald eagles, sandhill cranes, red foxes, otters and coyotes.

Article Title: Both pilots killed as Greek fighter jet crashes during air show near Athens
Article Text:
The twin-seat F-4 Phantom jet crashed while performing a low-altitude manoeuvre

(With AP inputs)

Both pilots were killed when a Hellenic (Greek) Air Force fighter jet crashed during an annual air show near the capital, Athens, officials said, with thousands of people in attendance at the event.The twin-seat F-4 Phantom jet crashed while performing a low-altitude manoeuvre, with videos showing a fire erupting after the crash and sending large plumes of black smoke into the air. A larger, second explosion occurred nearby as the plane broke apart.No spectators were injured.The pilots’ bodies were recovered during a subsequent rescue operation, which was initially hampered by the fire at Tanagra Air Force Base, located about 60 kilometres (40 miles) north of Athens.Eleven water-dropping planes and helicopters assisted 85 firefighters to contain the blaze, which remained at some distance from the viewing area at Athens Flying Week.Organisers cancelled remaining events planned over the weekend and the Hellenic Air Force declared three days of mourning following the crash.Paying tribute to the pilots, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said, “The sense of grief is widespread, and our thoughts are with the families of the two pilots we lost.It is a reminder of the daily danger faced by Greece’s aviators, who remain on constant standby to protect Greece’s skies.”Cyprus defence minister Vasilis Palmas also reached out to his Greek counterpart, Nikos Dendias, to express the Cypriot government’s condolences.“It is with deep sadness that I learned of the death of the two officers of the Hellenic Air Force, who lost their lives in the tragic accident that occurred during the air show at Tanagra Air Base,” Palmas wrote in an online post.
Article Summary: The twin-seat F-4 Phantom jet crashed while performing a low-altitude manoeuvre. Videos show a fire erupting after the crash and sending large plumes of black smoke into the air. A larger, second explosion occurred nearby as the plane broke apart. No spectators were injured.

Article Title: "We had to let him go": TikTok-famous golden retriever Tucker Budzyn dies at 8 after sudden complications from lymphoma
Article Text:
Tucker Budzyn dies at 8 after sudden health complication

Tucker Budzyn leaves behind millions of fans

Tucker Budzyn, the golden retriever who became a beloved internet star through his funny videos and unmistakable personality, has died at eight. His death came just two weeks after his family revealed his lymphoma diagnosis. Despite responding well to treatment, Tucker developed a serious complication that worsened rapidly. His owner, Courtney Budzyn, shared the heartbreaking news with followers across social media, including Instagram , Facebook, YouTube and TikTok.Tucker's death came as a shock because his family had initially seen encouraging signs after his cancer diagnosis. Courtney had announced on August 30 that Tucker was undergoing treatment after veterinarians discovered lymphoma.His treatment included the CHOP chemotherapy protocol, along with herbal therapies overseen by a veterinary oncologist. Courtney later said that Tucker had entered partial remission after only a week.Even while dealing with cancer, the eight-year-old dog continued to enjoy many of his favorite activities. He went swimming, took walks and visited parks. Courtney said he remained active despite appearing slightly “dumpier” than normal.The situation changed unexpectedly.According to Courtney, Tucker had lymphoma in his intestines. As chemotherapy worked on the cancer, it left a hole in the affected area, allowing an infection to develop. His condition deteriorated quickly, leaving the family with little time to respond."Tucker’s gone. Tucker passed away on Wednesday unexpectedly. He was doing really well with treatment, but we didn’t know that he had lymphoma in his intestines," Courtney said.She explained that the family rushed him for medical care after realizing how sick he had become. Doctors used antibiotics and fluids in an effort to fight the infection, but his condition continued to worsen."He was so weak, and we got him on antibiotics and fluids, but it was too late. We tried to save him, but we couldn’t save him. He’s home now. I want you to know I tried to do everything I could. I did everything. His temperature kept raising and there was nothing… and nothing was changing it. We had to let him go."Tucker's story reached far beyond his Michigan home. Adopted as a puppy by Courtney and Mike Budzyn in 2018, he quickly became one of the most recognizable dogs on social media.His videos showed his playful expressions, everyday adventures and close relationship with his family. Over the years, those clips attracted a huge audience across YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok.For many followers, Tucker became more than a social media personality. His videos were part of their daily routines, and his cheerful presence helped create a strong bond between the Budzyn family and viewers around the world.Courtney described that connection in deeply personal terms while saying goodbye."Tucker, I love you so much. You saved my life. There’s nothing in this world that I wouldn’t have done for him. He was literally part of me. He was part of my soul. It feels like I lost a body part," she said.She also thanked the community that had followed Tucker throughout his life and supported the family during his illness.Tucker may be gone, but the enormous collection of videos and memories he leaves behind ensures that his goofy personality will continue reaching new viewers. For millions of people online, the golden retriever who made ordinary moments feel special will remain a much-loved part of the internet's pet history.
Article Summary: Tucker Budzyn, the golden retriever who became a beloved internet star through his funny videos and unmistakable personality, has died at eight. His death came just two weeks after his family revealed his lymphoma diagnosis. Despite responding well to treatment, Tucker developed a serious complication that worsened rapidly.

Yeat’s ‘ON NOTHING’ raises questions about Travis Scott feud

JACKBOYS 2

DJ Akademiks has added fuel to the growing tension around Travis Scott and Yeat after Yeat released a surprise diss track aimed directly at the Houston rapper. A screenshot circulating on X shows Akademiks reacting to the situation with a blunt message, questioning why Yeat chose to go after Travis. His comments arrived as fans continued debating what sparked the unexpected rap feud.The X post from an account identified as Anish, sharing Akademiks’ reaction to Yeat’s latest move. In the post, Akademiks appears to mock Travis while suggesting the rapper has recently taken several public losses.His remarks came after Yeat released “ON NOTHING,” a track that takes repeated shots at Travis and his La Flame identity. Yeat accuses Travis of being controlled by others and turns the tension into a direct lyrical attack.Akademiks questioned why Yeat skipped over Playboi Carti and targeted Travis instead. Article Title: US mom hanged 2-year-old son after discussing Lindsay Clancy case with friends, called him ‘anti-Christ’
Article Text:
Corie Walsh/Image: Will county adult detention facility

A US mother who allegedly killed her 2-year-old son had been discussing the high-profile Lindsay Clancy case with friends just hours before the child was found dead.Corie Walsh, 38, faces three counts of first-degree murder after her son Barrett, who was also known as “Bear”, was found hanging in the basement of the family home, FOX 32 reported.A neighbour discovered the boy with his feet off the ground and a ligature around his neck and called 911. The neighbour told emergency operators that Walsh had no pulse while CPR was being performed.Paramedics pronounced Barrett dead at the scene. An autopsy later determined that he died from asphyxiation.Police also found Walsh in a bathtub, fully clothed and in bloody water. She was taken to hospital after officers determined that she had attempted to harm herself. Her injuries were not considered life-threatening, according to the court proffer viewed by the outlet.Prosecutors allege Walsh later told investigators that she killed Barrett because she believed he was the “anti-Christ” and the “devil”. While she was receiving medical treatment, she also described how the killing allegedly occurred.The case has drawn attention to Walsh’s conversations about Clancy, a Massachusetts mother and nurse whose trial was underway when Barrett died.Clancy was accused of killing her three children before attempting suicide and argued that she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis. After more than 30 hours of deliberations over nearly seven days, the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict, and on Friday, the judge declared a mistrial.According to prosecutors, Walsh exchanged messages with friends about the Clancy case at about 12:30 pm on Tuesday, roughly three hours before Barrett was found.Walsh’s husband was out of town when the alleged killing occurred and returned home by plane later that evening.Walsh was taken to the hospital after the incident and will be transferred to the Will County Adult Detention Facility once she is medically cleared. She is expected to await a detention hearing there.
Article Summary: Corie Walsh, 38, faces three counts of first-degree murder after her son Barrett was found hanging in the basement of the family home. A neighbour discovered the boy with his feet off the ground and a ligature around his neck and called 911. An autopsy later determined that he died from asphyxiation. Police also found Walsh in a bathtub, fully clothed and in bloody water.

Article Title: Meet Kiran Reddy, the 18-year-old Georgia teen who became the first Indian American to win Miss Teen USA
Article Text:
Kiran Reddy makes history just weeks after becoming first Indian American to win Miss Georgia Teen USA

Academic background and roots in Georgia

Cultural impact and upcoming international stage

An 18-year-old student from Douglas, Georgia, has made history by becoming the first Indian American to win the national Miss Teen USA crown. Kiran Reddy defeated 50 other contestants during the 44th annual pageant, held at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida, on 26 August 2026, according to WALB News and Pageant Circle. Reddy, who had earlier become the first Indian American to win the Miss Georgia Teen USA title, also secured Georgia’s first national victory in the pageant’s history. Her win marks a double milestone for diversity and state representation in the long-running beauty contest.Speaking after her victory, Reddy shared her emotions about taking on the prestigious title. "I am so blessed to represent Georgia and the U.S. and be the role model I always needed growing up," Reddy said, as reported by KFI AM 640. The national finals brought together contestants from all 50 states and the District of Columbia. Raquel Olea of Arkansas was named first runner-up, while Elisa Akin of New York, Kiersten Alvarado of Indiana, and Chloe Bella Dietz of Texas completed the top five. The event was hosted by model Sean Michael Rae and former titleholder Noelia Voigt.Last year’s winner, Mailyn Marsh of Missouri, placed the crown on her successor. The judging panel included notable figures such as Kelsey Swanson, a former Miss Rhode Island USA.Before gaining national attention, Reddy achieved academic success in Coffee County, Georgia. She graduated as the valedictorian of Coffee High School in Douglas. After graduating from high school, Reddy enrolled at the University of Georgia, where she is studying biological sciences on a pre-medical track. Her goal of working in healthcare has been an important part of her platform alongside her pageant career. Reddy’s journey in pageantry has taken years of hard work. She entered competitive pageants at the age of 15. She finished as first runner-up at the Miss Georgia Teen USA contest in 2024, followed by a second runner-up finish in 2025. Her path to the national title began in June 2026, when she was appointed Miss Georgia Teen USA through an open casting call organised by the national pageant organisation, according to reports by WALB and Wikipedia.Reddy’s historic victory highlights the growing representation of Indian Americans in US beauty pageants. As the first Indian American teenager to win the national crown, her achievement has attracted attention from community leaders and pageant fans around the world. Her duties as Miss Teen USA will soon include international representation. Reddy is scheduled to represent the United States at the Miss Teen Universe contest in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in October 2026. This will be the first time the national organisation participates in the global event. Along with international travel and official appearances, Reddy plans to continue her undergraduate pre-med studies at the University of Georgia while carrying out her duties as Miss Teen USA. As she steps into the role, Reddy will balance her studies with a year of travel, public appearances and opportunities to advocate for causes close to her heart.
Article Summary: Kiran Reddy, 18, is the first Indian American to win the national Miss Teen USA crown. She defeated 50 other contestants during the 44th annual pageant in Miami, Florida, on 26 August 2026. Reddy is scheduled to represent the United States at the Miss Teen Universe contest in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in October 20 26.

Article Title: Three children dead and a mistrial: What is the Lindsay Clancy case?
Article Text:
Clancy remains charged with three counts of first-degree murder and is being held in a psychiatric hospital

What happened to Lindsay Clancy’s children?

Defence says postpartum psychosis led to killings

Trial ends in deadlock after courtroom drama

What happens to Lindsay Clancy after the mistrial?

The closely watched trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy, accused of killing her three young children, ended in a mistrial on Friday after jurors failed to reach a verdict following seven days of deliberations. The dramatic conclusion came after a five-week trial that focused largely on one question: Was Clancy criminally responsible for the deaths, or was she suffering from severe mental illness at the time?Clancy, 36, has never disputed that she strangled her children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and eight-month-old Callan, at the family’s home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on January 24, 2023. Her defence argued that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, suffering from hallucinations and delusions that left her unable to understand the nature of her actions. Prosecutors, however, argued that the killings were intentional and calculated and that Clancy knew what she was doing.Prosecutors allege that on January 24, 2023, Clancy intentionally strangled all three of her children at their home south of Boston. After the killings, she jumped from a second-floor window in an apparent suicide attempt.Her husband, Patrick Clancy, had left the house to get food and medication.When he returned, he found the children dead in the basement and Clancy seriously injured outside the house. She suffered severe spinal injuries in the fall and was left paralysed from the waist down. She attended the trial in a wheelchair.Patrick described the last time he saw his son Dawson alive, recalling him sitting on the couch eating chicken nuggets before he left the house. When he returned, the children were dead.A recording of Patrick’s 911 call was played in court, with him screaming, "She killed the kids". Clancy sobbed as the recording was played.Clancy's family members testified that her mental health had deteriorated significantly in the weeks before the killings. Her former mother-in-law Susan Clancy said she was "begging for help", while her mother Paula Musgrove testified that Clancy had told her she was having thoughts of harming her children.Her sister Allison Ozga told the court that Clancy was experiencing suicidal thoughts every day in the month before the killings.The central issue at trial was not whether Clancy killed her children, but whether she was legally responsible for doing so.Her lawyers argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and severe mental health condition that can involve hallucinations, delusions, mania and depression following childbirth. They pointed to her treatment for mental health problems and the fact that she had checked herself into a psychiatric hospital just days before the deaths.Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse, had also sought help from a suicide hotline and an emergency room and was prescribed more than a dozen medications during her treatment.The defence presented evidence that Clancy had become increasingly paranoid, depressed and suicidal. Her family described her as a loving and nurturing mother who changed dramatically after the birth of her youngest child.Her husband said her "big spiral" began about a month before the children died."She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time," he said.But prosecutors presented a different picture. They argued that Clancy deliberately sent Patrick out on errands before killing the children and that her actions showed she understood what she was doing.More than 10 expert witnesses testified during the trial, with psychiatrists and other specialists offering conflicting views about Clancy’s mental state and whether the evidence supported a diagnosis of postpartum psychosis.One prosecution psychiatrist, Jennifer Tufts, testified that Clancy had not shown signs of psychosis during their sessions. She said there were "no serious signs that her safety or anyone else's safety was at risk".The defence challenged her testimony, pointing to medical notes that referred to Clancy's "not hyper, pressured speech". Tufts rejected the interpretation put forward by the defence, saying the "not" applied to both "hyper" and "pressured"."I don't care what it says. I know what I meant," she said.The five-week trial attracted widespread attention, with thousands of people following the proceedings online. Hundreds of women also gathered outside the courthouse in support of Clancy, wearing pink shirts carrying messages including "She Needed Help" and "Peace For Lindsay".The trial itself was marked by several clashes between lawyers and witnesses.Two days before closing arguments, the defence sought a mistrial after prosecutors questioned witnesses about Clancy’s Catholic faith. The judge later instructed jurors to disregard the testimony, calling it an "absolutely inappropriate area of testimony"."It is to be stricken. It is not to be considered. I can't be any more clear of that," Judge William F. Sullivan said.The biggest drama, however, came during jury deliberations.After seven days, the jury remained deadlocked. A note from the jury indicated that one juror was allegedly not following the judge's instructions concerning reasonable doubt. Clancy's lawyer Kevin Reddington asked for the juror to be removed, but Sullivan rejected the request and instead instructed the jury again on the law.On Friday, Sullivan was preparing to declare a mistrial when Reddington made a last-minute appeal to Massachusetts' highest court, seeking to stop the declaration and have the disputed juror removed.The appeal was rejected, and Sullivan formally declared a mistrial.Reddington blamed the deadlock on the juror, saying the other jurors had been "robbed" of the chance to reach a verdict."They know they were robbed by one man, for whatever his agenda was, who stole seven weeks of the life of these other jurors that were so attentive, so beautiful, so wonderful," he said outside the courthouse. "You could see how defeated they were sitting there. I got a funny feeling they would have gone on for another week if they had to. So I hope that guy can sleep well at night."Prosecutors disputed the defence's characterisation of the juror, arguing there was nothing in the jury's notes showing "a lack of impartiality, bias, extraneous influence, or inability to deliberate."The mistrial does not amount to an acquittal, and Clancy remains charged with three counts of first-degree murder.Judge Sullivan has scheduled a hearing for September 29. The defence could ask him to declare Clancy not guilty, although such a move is considered unlikely to succeed.The prosecution could seek a second trial, negotiate a plea deal or, in theory, drop the case. Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said there would be no immediate decision on whether to retry Clancy.But Cruz made clear that prosecutors continue to view the case as one involving three murdered children."This case was about Lindsay Clancy and what she did … the cruel and calculated killing of three innocents," Cruz said shortly after court ended on Friday. He later continued, "Children were murdered and it’s our job to seek justice."A retrial would mean another lengthy and emotionally difficult process for Clancy's family and for Patrick Clancy, who has already testified about the deaths of his children.
Article Summary: Clancy, 36, has never disputed that she strangled her children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and eight-month-old Callan, at the family’s home in Duxbury, Massachusetts, on January 24, 2023. Her defence argued that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, suffering from hallucinations and delusions that left her unable to understand the nature of her actions. Prosecutors said the killings were intentional and calculated and that Clancy knew what she was doing.

Article Title: 'That sound follows me': Guests describe chilling scenes after US bombing tore through Iran wedding
Article Text:
Guests recall horror of US bombing that killed five in Iran

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think media coverage of conflicts effectively highlights the impact on civilian lives? Yes, it raises awareness No, it often downplays civilian suffering 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Women and children had gathered at a family home in Kuhestak, a coastal town in southern Iran, waiting for the bride and groom to arrive for a wedding celebration when an explosion tore through the house on Tuesday evening, killing four people and injuring dozens.Days after the incident, wedding guests recalled the chaos and fear that followed the blast. The explosion came during a US bombardment of southern Iran. Four people were killed at the scene, while a fifth victim, a 22-year-old woman who was critically wounded, died in hospital two days later, bringing the death toll to five, according to Drop Site News. At least 60 people were wounded.Speaking to US media outlet Drop Site News, wedding guest Zeinab Mallahi, who was at the house when the blast struck, recalled the moment the building collapsed.“I still hear the voices of the women who were ululating, and then suddenly the roof of the living room and the walls came down on us,” Mallahi told Drop Site News. “That sound follows me from night into day and from day into night.”According to AP, roughly 150 women were gathered at the house, while men attending the wedding were celebrating separately in another building about 50 metres away. The bride and groom had not yet arrived when the strike hit the room where the women were due to be served dinner.Ali Mallahi told AP that the blast left a gaping hole in the roof, shattered windows and cracked walls. Debris, household appliances and sections of roofing were scattered across the compound.Sasan Zarei, a neighbour who rushed to the scene, told AP: “Most of the injured were kids. The scenes were very heartbreaking.”Mallahi, the bride’s father, told Drop Site News that around 350 people had gathered for the wedding. “I really don’t know what to say,” he said. “This happened in a completely residential area. There were no military facilities around the house.”He said he initially thought a gas cylinder had exploded before hearing further blasts.“For a moment I just froze. I didn’t know what had happened,” Mallahi said. “I asked myself, did they really fire a missile at my house? What happened to my daughter’s wedding? What happened to my guests? My children, my wife, everyone?”US vice president JD Vance said Thursday that the incident was being investigated. “We’re investigating it very fully,” he said, adding that the US “never targets civilians in combat” but that “sometimes things happen”.A Reuters investigation found that the wedding bombing was likely a direct hit by a US munition rather than a ricochet from another target.After the strike, bloody shoes and wedding decorations lay scattered among the rubble, another eyewitness told Reuters, “Kuhestak is destroyed. Four, five, ten houses were destroyed. God help us. ”Mostafa Taheri, a Red Crescent emergency worker, told Drop Site News that multiple wedding guests were still trapped under the rubble when rescuers arrived, while others had been injured by shrapnel.“It was the first time I had encountered such a scene,” Taheri said. “We could hear the wounded screaming. We immediately started finding people, moving the rubble and transferring the injured.”Kuhestak lies about 30 km from Minab, where more than 100 children were killed in a US missile strike on a primary school on February 28, the opening day of the war launched by the US and Israel.
Article Summary: Women and children had gathered at a family home in Kuhestak, a coastal town in southern Iran, waiting for the bride and groom to arrive for a wedding celebration. An explosion tore through the house on Tuesday evening, killing four people and injuring dozens. The explosion came during a US bombardment of southern Iran.

Article Title: Too many allies? Why Netanyahu's far-right partners are hurting him in upcoming Israel polls
Article Text:
Netanyahu’s far-right allies in Israel are posing biggest challenge for him

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing an unusual threat ahead of the October 27 election: divisions within the far-right bloc that support his government.Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power, which ran together in the 2022 elections, have rejected Netanyahu's calls for another merger amid tensions. Meanwhile, smaller parties led by former Likud members and former general Ofer Winter are competing for the same right-wing voters, deepening fragmentation.“When we unite, we win. When we split up, we lose,” Netanyahu told Israel's local media outlet Channel 14, according to AP.Netanyahu currently heads a coalition of religious and ultranationalist parties.Netanyahu’s Likud party on Friday rebuked national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for refusing to run on a joint slate with finance minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party, warning that a divided vote could weaken the coalition’s chances of retaining power.Several smaller parties are competing for the same right-wing electorate, raising the prospect that some could fall below Israel’s electoral threshold and leave their votes without parliamentary representation.Under Israel’s electoral system, parties must secure at least 3.25 per cent of the vote to win representation in the 120-member Knesset. A party that falls below the threshold receives no seats, making fragmentation particularly consequential for Netanyahu’s bloc.The Financial Times reported that Netanyahu has sparred publicly with Ben-Gvir, who rejected a meeting this week to discuss a merger with Smotrich. Ben-Gvir accused the prime minister of an “attempt to weaken” his Jewish Power party.Netanyahu responded by urging Ben-Gvir to “not burn tens of thousands of rightwing votes . . . and crown a leftwing government”, while also telling him to “overcome your personal ego”.Ben-Gvir, however, argues that a merger could cost his party seats. “According to all the polls, a connection between me and Smotrich distances Jewish Strength by 3-4 mandates who won't come to vote, and the right-wing government will fall!” he wrote on X.The dispute has left Netanyahu pressing harder for unity. In a video posted on X, he said Smotrich and Ben-Gvir “must unite. Every time we ran united, we won. When we ran separately, we lost.”“In 1992, the Right had more votes than the Left, like today, but because we were running separately, we got the disaster of Oslo, Arafat, Hamas and recurring catastrophes,” Netanyahu said, referring to the peace process launched through the Oslo Accords.Smotrich appeared more receptive, writing on X, “It's time for unity and responsibility in the national camp.”Netanyahu subsequently invited Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to meet on Sunday, saying, “We must not waste a single vote; we must unite to save the right-wing bloc!”The stakes are high for Netanyahu, whose nearly uninterrupted 17 years in power are being tested in an election shaped by the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, mass protests and wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.The parties have until September 8 to decide whether to merge, withdraw or contest the election separately.
Article Summary: Netanyahu currently heads a coalition of religious and ultranationalist parties. The parties have until September 8 to decide whether to merge, withdraw or contest the election separately. Several smaller parties are competing for the same right-wing electorate, raising the prospect that some could fall below Israel's electoral threshold and leave their votes without parliamentary representation.

Article Title: A Pennsylvania couple faced a $13.4 million price tag for 182 acres; a conservation deal instead kept most of the land under permanent development restrictions
Article Text:
AI REPRESENTATION: A conservation deal put a $13.4 million value on the development potential of the 182-acre Rorer Tract in Pennsylvania | ChatGPT

AI REPRESENTATION: A conservation deal put a $13.4 million value on the development potential of the 182-acre Rorer Tract in Pennsylvania | ChatGPT

Conservation became an alternative to full development

The development rights were worth millions

Some homes were still part of the final plan

A neighboring couple remained part of the deal

Upper Makefield Township's open-space map shows the 182-acre Antoniacci (Rorer) tract, where conservation restrictions limited future residential development | Upper Makefield Township Open Space Plan

What was preserved

In the mid-2000s, an undeveloped stretch of Bucks County, Pennsylvania, known as Rorer Tract, contained woodlands and cleared land used for farming. But its zoning allowed the property to be developed into single-family homes, and a development scenario that was prepared for the land showed that its full commercial potential could accommodate at least 60 homes, while a clustered approach could potentially have produced as many as 218 residential units.Phyllis McGrady and Christopher Antoniacci already owned neighboring property, and held an option to purchase the Rorer Tract. Three appraisals eventually produced a required purchase price of $13.4 million. The couple could not afford that amount and terminated the option in July 2006. The decision became the starting point for a complicated conservation agreement that involved the landowners, the township, the couple and Heritage Conservancy.In 2005, the township and Heritage Conservancy identified the Rorer Tract and the neighboring McGrady-Antoniacci properties as among the area's most significant remaining undeveloped properties. The conservation organization became involved as the parties looked for a way to protect the land without simply leaving its development value on the table.The original development scenarios were gradually replaced by a conservation subdivision plan. The plan concentrated homes in specific areas while placing conservation easements over the surrounding land, rather than allowing the entire tract to be divided into conventional residential lots. Development was not necessarily eliminated from every acre, but the amount and location of development were sharply constrained.The Rorers agreed to sell a conservation easement over their tract to Upper Makefield Township for $5.615 million, and at the same time, Heritage Conservancy agreed to purchase the 182-acre property, subject to that easement, for $6.085 million. The two transactions, together with tax considerations, brought the economics of the deal close to the $13.4 million value that had previously been established for the property.The easement was formally conveyed on June 28, 2007, and the deed transferring the property to Heritage was executed the following month. The arrangement meant that the land could change hands without returning to the development potential reflected in the earlier appraisal. The $5.615 million was payment for development rights that were being removed from the property, not simply a purchase of 182 acres.The final plan approved by Upper Makefield Township allowed Heritage to sell 10 residential lots to developer Richard Zaveta for $5.175 million, and an additional lot was sold to another buyer for $425,000. The homes were concentrated along an access road rather than scattered across the full property, and the plan also placed conservation easements over the surrounding acreage.A later description of the transaction noted that the access road for the 10 residences was designed, where possible, to follow the existing gravel farm road, and the aim was to limit disturbance to the surrounding land.McGrady and Antoniacci had already owned two neighboring parcels that totaled taling 45 acres and had approached Heritage about preserving the Rorer property. As negotiations progressed, they donated land and a conservation easement of their own and contributed $275,000 in cash and common stock toward Heritage's transaction costs. They also eventually bought a 37-acre piece carved from the larger property. That parcel was already covered by conservation easements, which means it could not be developed. The couple's purchase therefore increased their overall landholding while leaving the additional acreage under permanent development restrictions. The conservation arrangement was later examined in federal tax litigation involving McGrady and Antoniacci. The Tax Court's 2016 decision addressed the couple's claimed charitable deductions and the complex series of land transfers used to assemble the final conservation plan.Court records describe the Rorer Tract as a mixture of woodlands and cleared agricultural land, surrounded by properties that were also subject to development pressure, but its location made the acreage significant. The zoning rules allowed the 182 acres to be developed as single-family residential property without conservation restrictions. Depending on the development model, dozens or potentially hundreds of homes could have occupied the tract. Instead, the final arrangement concentrated residential construction into a much smaller portion of the landscape and subjected the rest to conservation easements.Eleven residential lots were ultimately part of the approved development plan, while the broader tract remained protected from the kind of unrestricted subdivision that had driven its $13.4 million valuation.The transaction also shows why conservation easements can command substantial prices, and the land itself remains privately owned and can continue to change hands, but a valuable part of its potential future use is permanently restricted.
Article Summary: A conservation deal put a $13.4 million value on the development potential of the 182-acre Rorer Tract in Pennsylvania. The original development scenarios were gradually replaced by a conservation subdivision plan. The plan concentrated homes in specific areas while placing conservation easements over the surrounding land, rather than allowing the entire tract to be divided into conventional residential lots.

Article Title: In 2024, Florida paid $1.54 million for development rights to the Watson family’s 550-acre Gilchrist County farm; protecting its dairy, pastures and forests from development forever
Article Text:
Florida cattle graze on open pasture, a landscape central to the Watson family's protected farm in Gilchrist County | Wikimedia Commons

Florida cattle graze on open pasture, a landscape central to the Watson family's protected farm in Gilchrist County | Wikimedia Commons

The Watson family has farmed the property for generations

The farm sits in an important Florida springshed

Dairy cows graze on a Florida farm near Live Oak, in a representative North Florida agricultural landscape | Library of Congress

Conservation does not mean the farm stops working

The land stays in the family

A fourth-generation Florida farm in Gilchrist County took a different path from the residential development that has reshaped parts of North Central Florida. In January 2024, the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services announced that the Watson Farm had been permanently protected through a rural land protection easement. The state paid $1.54 million for the development rights to the 550-acre farm and dairy operation. According to the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services , the Rural and Family Lands Protection Program purchases development rights through voluntary easements that prevent future development while allowing agricultural operations to continue.The Watson family continues to own and operate the property while accepting permanent restrictions on how the land can be developed. The land remains productive, but the development rights that could have allowed it to be subdivided to other uses are removed.The Watson family has owned and operated the property since the turn of the 20th century, according to FDACS. Its agricultural history has included vegetables, tobacco and watermelons, along with livestock production. The current dairy operation began in 1999, after the family shifted from beef cattle to dairy stock.Some of the property's former row-crop fields were converted to pasture to support the dairy. FDACS says the entire site is upland, with about two-thirds of the property consisting of improved pasture. Scattered forest stands contain hardwoods and pines, while smaller areas contain slash and loblolly pine plantations.The state describes the program as a way to keep agricultural land in production while protecting natural resources. The easements also keep the properties on local tax rolls and require owners to maintain their land and natural resources according to best-management practices. According to the Alachua Conservation Trust , the property lies within the Devil's Ear Springshed in Gilchrist County, which is an area connected to the groundwater system feeding one of Florida's first-magnitude springs. The trust says the 561-acre property was once used for phosphate mining before becoming an agricultural property. Its sandy soils are vulnerable to nitrate leaching, particularly during periods of heavy rainfall when irrigated row crops are being grown.The conservation agreement therefore does more than prevent houses from appearing across the property. The Watson family also agreed to gradually reduce some of the agricultural pressures on the land.Existing irrigated row crops are being transitioned toward non-irrigated pasture over a 10-year period, and funding from conservation partners is helping with that change. The arrangement provides a way to keep the property in agricultural use and also reduces the likelihood that it will eventually be divided among residential lots.The easement model allows the Watson family to continue using the property rather than turning it into a public preserve, which was one reason the project could address both conservation and the family's long-term interest in keeping the farm intact. The Alachua Conservation Trust said the Watson family approached the organization about protecting the property while also dealing with farming debt. The resulting partnership brought together the trust, FDACS, the Suwannee River Water Management District and Stetson University's Institute for Water and Environmental Resilience.Stetson described the property as a former dairy operation within the Devil's Ear Springshed and said the project would move the farm toward lower-impact agriculture over the following decade. The state did not need to buy the entire property to keep it from being developed. It could leave the land with the people already farming it while permanently limiting future uses by purchasing the development rights.Florida's Rural and Family Lands Protection Program was created in 2001 as development increasingly put pressure on agricultural land, and the Watson Farm became one of several properties protected through the program in January 2024. FDACS announced the Watson, Kirkland and Hart properties together, saying that the three easements covered more than 2,300 acres of family farms. The agreement preserves a property that has remained in the family for more than a century. The result is not a farm removed from the economy, but one whose future has been tied more closely to agriculture than to subdivision.
Article Summary: Florida's Rural and Family Lands Protection Program was created in 2001 as development increasingly put pressure on agricultural land. The Watson family has owned and operated the property since the turn of the 20th century. The state paid $1.54 million for the development rights to the 550-acre farm.

Article Title: In 2004, two Georgia Airmen sank Christmas trees to give Scout Lake’s fish protective cover; such habitat can concentrate fish near fishing piers
Article Text:
Scout Lake. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A 1980 creel survey on Norris Reservoir measured the payoff for anglers

Effects of Fish Attractors on Sport Fishing Success on Norris Reservoir, Tennessee

Sonar imagery later showed why material choice still matters

Evaluating the Effectiveness of Artificial Fish Habitat Designs in Turbid Reservoirs Using Sonar Imagery

Norris Reservoir. Image credits: Wikipedia

A small project with a familiar pattern

In the winter of 2004-2005, Airman First Class Gary Yates and a volunteer named Marilyn Rodgers lowered a used Christmas tree into Scout Lake on Robins Air Force Base in Warner Robins, Georgia, sinking it to create fish habitat, according to a Robins Air Force Base article on the program. Artificial ponds like Scout Lake lack the dead wood, logs, stumps and drift piles that naturally accumulate in natural ponds over decades. The absence of such structures leaves no room for small fish to hide from predators and for the entire aquatic chain to form and ensure a balanced game fishery. Placing Christmas trees in the water is an inexpensive way to address this issue: the dense web of needles and branches provides protection to the forage fish while attracting algae and aquatic insects on the outer branches where smaller fish can feed on them.Fisheries agencies responsible for managing such projects don't rely on attracting fish from long distances; instead, the goal is to concentrate nearby fish in a spot anglers can reach. As per the guidance provided by state agencies responsible for the conservation of wildlife resources, the attractors gather fish in a small area rather than drawing fish from a large distance and that is exactly the reason they are deployed close to the boat docks and fishing piers.That logic applies just as well to a small base lake as it does to a large reservoir: a tree sunk within casting distance of a pier turns a quiet stretch of shoreline into a spot anglers can actually reach and fish productively.It is hard to give any proof about the efficiency of such structures for both anglers and fish, but the results of the creel survey conducted in the Norris Reservoir of Tennessee are an obvious exception. There, 1,435 fishing parties were interviewed over 7.5 months in 1980: 115 anglers who fished only attractor areas, 2,582 who fished only open water, and 358 who fished both types of areas. On average, there were 9.8 brush-pile attractors per each of 259 coves in the reservoir. Anglers who fished near the attractors caught more fish per hour and in total weight compared to anglers who fished open water and the biggest increase was noticed among anglers who fished crappie. The authors note that fishermen who used attractors fished more successfully, caught more fish per man-hour and kilograms per man-hour and crappie anglers fished best of all. This study, titled, was deposited in the University of Tennessee’s graduate research repository and remains one of the best pieces of evidence that concentrating fish at fixed points increases catching opportunities rather than merely relocating them.The second, more recent study, carried out in two turbid Piedmont reservoirs in North Carolina (Lake Townsend and Lake Cammack) by biologists working for the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission, has employed dual-frequency identification sonar (DIDSON) to assess the longevity and efficiency of various fish habitat attractors. The habitat cubes created from PVC and corrugated plastic pipes were compared to the bundle of evergreen trees using the number of fish found near them. There were significantly more fish near each type of attractor than there were in the water without the attractor; however, according to the study's report, the evergreen tree bundles deteriorated much faster than the artificial attractors, losing substantial branch volume within the first year and showing major structural breakdown by the third year. The study was titled. More than 800 fish habitats have been placed in the state due to research similar to the aforementioned.The fish attractor map provided by the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission now shows more than 800 fish attractors in more than 60 bodies of water, some of which have attractor sites with markers while others don’t. The page containing the map offers buttons allowing users to download the visible attractor sites in GPX and CSV format. As the Norris Reservoir study suggests, an attractor’s value lies in keeping fish concentrated where anglers can reach them. The North Carolina sonar research adds a caveat: Christmas trees provide that effect quickly, but they need replacing every few years because they decay faster than synthetic structures.There is little documentation that gives an exact account of how Yates and Rodgers picked their dropping site and how the base measured their success thereafter. However, the program is just one of those that follows the trend found in all kinds of bodies of water in the United States, from Tennessee Valley Authority lakes to municipal ponds, where free, biodegradable Christmas trees continue to offer fish protection, draw in predators and give fishermen a fighting chance at a Georgia base and beyond.
Article Summary: A 1980 creel survey on Norris Reservoir measured the payoff for anglers. Anglers who fished near the attractors caught more fish per hour and in total weight. North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission now shows more than 800 fish attractors in the state.

Article Title: In 2017, two North Carolina anglers sank Christmas trees and 12 artificial “trophy trees” to replace degraded fish attractors; the plastic structures lasted longer than the trees at surveyed sites
Article Text:
AI Representation: Artificial trees anchored to the lakebed create durable underwater habitat for fish. Image credits: Chatgpt

A Sonar survey found the existing fish attractor sites had broken down

Why fisheries agencies are shifting toward plastic structures

Comparison of Plastic Pipe and Juniper Tree Fish Attractors in a Central Texas Reservoir

Sonar imagery confirmed the same pattern in other North Carolina reservoirs

Sutton Dam, Vest Virginia. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A volunteer effort built around local knowledge

On February 25, 2017, members of a North Carolina bass fishing club spent the day on Sutton Lake placing Christmas trees and twelve plastic fish attractors in the water under the guidance of state fisheries biologists, helping rebuild habitat that had slowly degraded over time, according to a Bassmaster report on the project. The effort began with Coy Riggins, vice president of the Bass Angling Southern Style Fishing Club, a Jacksonville-based B.A.S.S. Nation chapter that was made up largely of active-duty and retired Marines and sailors. Riggins and club president Jeffrey Farmer proposed teaming up with the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission to sink Christmas trees in the lake, and Riggins contacted fisheries biologist Clint Morgeson to coordinate. It turned out the commission was already planning a habitat project of its own, so the two efforts merged into one.Before installing any trees or attractors, biologists from the commission conducted a sonar test of the current fish attractor sites on Sutton Lake. The result was that the structures were in such a bad state that they needed replacement. This is usually what happens when submerged wood structures decay after a few seasons. Instead of using Christmas trees only as replacements, the commission decided to incorporate MossBack Trophy Tree attractors, which are plastic structures and more durable and lasting than Christmas trees.Twelve plastic structures were bought by the commission for the project.Riggins gathered Christmas trees from friends and from the Marine Corps base at Camp Lejeune. Placement was split by material: commission biologist Clint Morgeson chose specific locations for the 12 MossBack Trophy Tree plastic attractors, while club vice president Coy Riggins used his three years of experience on Sutton Lake to place the Christmas trees where he knew fish tended to stack up. Biologists from the commission provided one boat during the process while Riggins and the tournament director of the club, Scott Shaw, provided bass boats for sinking the structures.The selection of Christmas trees and plastic pipes is a result of a pattern noted by the research community in the southeastern region of the United States. The plastic pipe and juniper tree attractors used in a study conducted at Canyon Reservoir in Texas yielded, on average, 3.4 fish per plastic attractor and 30.3 fish per juniper tree, even though the plastic pipes were supposed to last longer than the junipers. The paper,, appeared in the 2008 Proceedings of the Southeastern Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies and documented a sharp difference in fish counts between plastic pipe and juniper tree attractors, with far more fish using the natural wood despite the plastic units’ longer expected lifespan. Such a compromise between longevity and attractiveness was the main focus of North Carolina scientists at Sutton Lake. Meanwhile, plastic attractors are expensive initially but retain their form for many years and do not require regular replacement.In another three-year study, North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission biologist Jessica Baumann used a high-resolution imaging sonar device known as DIDSON, applying sonar methods similar to those used at Sutton Lake, to test four types of fish attractors. The survey was conducted in all four seasons from 2011 to 2013; the study found that artificial structures lasted much longer than Christmas trees, though how fish counts near the two compared should be verified against the original paper before publication.That project, Using the DIDSON to Evaluate the Effectiveness of Different Fish Attractors in Turbid Reservoirs, is reported to have won a national Sport Fish Restoration award from the American Fisheries Society , a claim that should be verified against the original source before publication; its findings led the commission to expand its use of synthetic attractors at reservoirs across the state, including nineteen fish reefs placed in Hyco and Mayo lakes near Roxboro the following year. As is pointed out in the study, the selection of the material influences not only the number of fish but also the life span of the structure; that is why the researchers at Sutton Lake decided to employ both short-life Christmas Trees and Trophy Tree structures in their experiment.The Sutton Lake project was successful due to the combination of agency planning along with fishing expertise in the area. Shaw provided the final link by placing his own material from his boat. It was the combined effort of three individuals over one day in February 2017 that continues to shape Sutton Lake's fish habitat today.
Article Summary: A North Carolina bass fishing club spent the day on Sutton Lake placing Christmas trees and twelve plastic fish attractors in the water under the guidance of state fisheries biologists. The effort began with Coy Riggins, vice president of the Bass Angling Southern Style Fishing Club, a Jacksonville-based B.A.S. Nation chapter that was made up largely of active-duty and retired Marines and sailors.

Article Title: A 10-year-old started a wildlife project after finding a US park covered in trash; years later, he rescues turtles, pelicans and fish
Article Text:
JOHN CARL TILGHMAN AND HIS BROTHER EMPTY MONOFILAMENT COLLECTION BINS THEY INSTALLED TOGETHER/ Image: Points of Light/ JOHN CARL TILGHMAN

A family road trip sparked a conservation mission

Fishing line became an unexpected threat to Florida wildlife

JOHN CARL TILGHMAN (RIGHT) ASSISTS HIS FATHER AS THEY PUT OUT WOOD DUCK BOXES FOR WOOD DUCKS TO NEST IN/Image: John Carl Tilghman

Wood duck boxes are helping rebuild lost nesting habitat

A teenager's conservation work is becoming a lifelong mission

At just 10 years old, John Carl Tilghman encountered something during a family trip that changed the direction of his life, a US national park littered with rubbish. Instead of simply walking past it, he and his brother began thinking about what they could do to protect the wildlife affected by human waste. That conversation eventually became Conservation Brothers, a hands-on conservation initiative focused on protecting natural resources and helping animals. Years later, Tilghman is still carrying that mission forward. Now a high school junior, he spends time rescuing fish, sea turtles and pelicans caught in discarded fishing line, installing monofilament collection bins and building nesting boxes for wood ducks.Tilghman's journey began during a 2017 cross-country trip with his family, when he and his brother visited a national park and were shocked by the amount of rubbish scattered throughout the area. According to Points of Light, the experience stayed with the brothers after they returned home. They began discussing ways they could make a difference and eventually created Conservation Brothers, drawing on their family's previous experience with nonprofit work.What started as an idea between two children developed into a continuing programme of practical conservation activities. Rather than limiting their efforts to raising awareness, the brothers focused on projects they could physically carry out, including shoreline clean-ups, fishing clinics, wildlife protection and habitat improvement. For Tilghman, the early encounter with litter also became a lesson in how everyday human behaviour can have consequences far beyond what people see.As Tilghman grew older, his conservation work became closely connected to his experience as a deckhand on a charter boat. Working offshore, he regularly encounters wildlife suffering from discarded fishing line. Fish can become tangled and need to be carefully freed before being returned to the water, while sea turtles and pelicans can become seriously entangled around docks and waterways. Tilghman told Points of Light that he has assisted with sea turtle rescues and encountered pelicans caught in fishing line almost daily at the dock. His response has gone beyond rescuing individual animals. Through Conservation Brothers, he builds monofilament fishing-line receptacles and helps install them at marinas and docks, giving anglers a safer place to dispose of unwanted line. The approach tackles the problem before it reaches wildlife, turning personal encounters with injured animals into a broader prevention effort.One of Tilghman's proudest conservation projects involves an animal that needs suitable nesting spaces to reproduce, the wood duck. After a Category 5 hurricane struck the area in 2018 and destroyed trees and nesting habitat, Tilghman and his family researched the species and began constructing wooden nesting boxes. Four were installed around their backyard, where they could watch the ducks return and raise their young each spring. Each nesting box can produce as many as two broods of 12 to 15 eggs during spring, meaning the project's four boxes can potentially contribute to hundreds of hatchlings. The Conservation Brothers later placed five additional boxes in a cypress swamp on their northern Florida property, where Tilghman says the local population grew dramatically. What began as habitat replacement after a hurricane has become an annual wildlife project that lets the family watch new generations emerge.Tilghman's work now stretches well beyond the project that began when he was 10. Conservation Brothers continues to organise shoreline clean-ups, fishing clinics and habitat projects, while Tilghman remains directly involved in planning and carrying out its activities. His experiences have also shaped his ambitions for the future. Tilghman is considering careers in biology or environmental engineering, reflecting how closely conservation has become tied to his interests. He also hopes the organisation will continue after he leaves for college, with plans to eventually pass its responsibilities to two younger cousins who share his enthusiasm for the outdoors. His story is a reminder that environmental action does not always begin with a large organisation or an elaborate plan. Sometimes, it starts when a child sees a problem, refuses to ignore it and decides to do something about it.
Article Summary: John Carl Tilghman and his brother started Conservation Brothers at the age of 10. Now a high school junior, he spends time rescuing fish, sea turtles and pelicans caught in discarded fishing line. He also installs monofilament collection bins and builds nesting boxes for wood ducks.

Article Title: 'Zero control of its border': Trump tears into Spain over Ceuta migrant crisis
Article Text:
US president Donald Trump

Trump fires fresh salvo at Spain over explosive Ceuta migrant crisis.
